strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10+ model families, 4+ datasets, and 4 different advantage estimation methods with consistent 3-10% improvements
Clever sparsification scheme that maintains 99.999% probability mass with only 5-10 tokens, making trust region projections tractable for large vocabularies
Principled approach replacing heuristic clipping with theoretically grounded KL-based trust regions, with rigorous sparsification bounds (Theorem A.2)
Practical drop-in replacement for PPO clipping with modest computational overhead (4-10%) and no inference-time cost
Excellent reproducibility: detailed mathematical derivations, pseudocode, hyperparameter documentation, ablation studies, and promised code release
Successfully stabilizes GSPO where clipping diverges entirely, demonstrating practical impact beyond marginal improvements
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core technique (Lagrangian dual optimization for trust region projections) is from Otto et al. (2021); main contribution is adapting to discrete LLM distributions with sparsification

Narrow experimental scope: all experiments focus exclusively on mathematical reasoning (DAPO, GSM8K, MATH); no evaluation on other RL-for-LLM domains (summarization, instruction following, alignment) despite claims of broad applicability
Lacks theoretical justification for why per-token KL constraints should outperform importance-ratio clipping; no convergence analysis or optimization landscape comparison
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compares against PPO clipping; missing comparisons with TRPO variants, DPO approaches, or other recent RLVR methods
Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some improvements (1-2%) may be within noise; limited discussion of variance across seeds

Ad-hoc design choices: regression term in Eq. 5 (with gradient clipping) lacks clear justification; hyperparameter defaults (α=1, K=64, δ=10^-5, p_d=10^-12) appear arbitrary; sensitivity to α not explored
Incomplete mechanistic analysis: why do both methods affect ~0.1% of tokens yet TROLL improves more? Why does TROLL preserve entropy? Underlying mechanisms for response length adaptation unclear
Computational overhead is non-trivial (4-10% memory, 9-17% runtime for small-to-medium models) and absolute costs matter in practice despite scaling benefits

strengths: Principled approach: Theoretically grounded alternative to heuristic PPO clipping using convex trust region projections
Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across multiple models (600M-14B), datasets (DAPO, GSM8K, Eurus, Math-Eval), and RL algorithms (GRPO, Dr.GRPO, PPO, GSPO, REINFORCE++)
Clever sparsification scheme: Reduces memory from ~1.16GiB to <1MiB while retaining 99.999% probability mass, with theoretical error bounds
Stability improvements: Enables training of methods like GSPO that diverge with standard clipping; faster convergence for multiple model families
Sound mathematical execution: Correct derivations of primal/dual solutions, proper implicit differentiation for backpropagation, rigorous error bound proofs
Thorough analysis and ablations: Systematic study of hyperparameters, batch size stability, entropy preservation, response length dynamics, and projection fractions
Practical implementation: Clean drop-in replacement for clipping with minimal inference overhead and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Primarily adapts Otto et al. (2021)'s trust region projections from continuous to discrete distributions; conceptual contribution is incremental
Narrow evaluation scope: Restricted to RLVR tasks (math and code generation); no evaluation on RLHF, preference-based methods, or other RL settings despite claims of broad applicability
Incomplete theoretical analysis: Lacks convergence guarantees, analysis versus original RL objective, or characterization of when/why TROLL helps beyond 'better trust region'

Ad-hoc regression term: Equation 5's KL regression term is borrowed from Otto et al. but rationale specific to LLMs and necessity are not well justified; stop-gradient operation partially breaks gradient flow
Sparsification heuristic: Greedy top-K selection is practical but heuristic; Theorem A.1 assumption about relative likelihood stability may not always hold
Hyperparameter tuning and choices: KL bound ϵ requires manual tuning with limited guidance; α set to 1 'for simplicity' but robustness claims not well supported
Computational overhead: Significant for smaller models (54% for 0.6B, 9-16% for 4B), potentially problematic in practice
Statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single runs reported (though smoothed); small datasets could have significant variance
Limited scope of generalization: Out-of-distribution evaluation (MATH-Eval) shows smaller improvements than in-distribution; generalization beyond current task settings unclear
Missing comparisons: No comparison with recent trust region or preference optimization methods beyond BAPO; no RLHF evaluation
